news.originalContent:
Israel’s president officially tasks the opposition leader with forming a new government.

Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, the man officially tasked by President Isaac Herzog with trying to form the country’s next government, has said that he was open to including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his coalition lineup.

In a speech at Sunday’s ceremony in Herzog’s office in Jerusalem, Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join.

“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said.

Eisenkot, who ran as Netanyahu’s main rival, has six weeks to form a new government. At the ceremony, Eisenkot said he will act in the interests of the public and represent all parts of Israeli society.

Herzog, meanwhile, warned that the country faced uncertainties after the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, which brought victories for several political figures critical of Israel and the US’s military support.

“The State of Israel needs a stable government,” Herzog said, pointing to the “new political reality” in the US.

Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Despite this, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate to replace Netanyahu.

In Israel’s October 27 elections, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats.

Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.

“Netanyahu still has time to derail Gadi Eisenkot’s efforts to form a government and sabotage attempts to gain a vote of confidence,” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank.

“In the meantime, he remains caretaker prime minister. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would be the natural second in line to be tasked with forming a government. And if he fails, elections would then be called, and that would still allow Netanyahu to remain as caretaker.

“Many of Netanyahu’s critics say that is his aim. The big question in Israeli politics now is: does the opposition really want to get rid of Netanyahu? Or is the opposition to Palestinian Israelis in mainstream politics so strong that they’re willing to risk keeping Netanyahu in power by going back to the ballot box?”

news.originalContent:
Kozo Tashima believes he has a ’20 to 30 percent’ chance of winning the FIFA presidency election against Infantino.

The latest challenger to FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid, Kozo Tashima, believes he has a 20 to 30 percent chance of winning the coveted seat in global football.

Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA), said governance is FIFA’s biggest problem as he outlined his platform for next year’s presidential election on Sunday.

“I’ve received many messages saying, ‘Thank you for speaking out’…,” Tashima told Japanese daily Sports Nippon.

Tashima announced on Thursday that he intended to run in the March election, becoming the first Japanese candidate to seek world football’s top job.

The 68-year-old former Japan international has served on the FIFA Council since 2015 and became JFA president the following year before being succeeded by Tsuneyasu Miyamoto in 2024.

“I’ve been contacted by presidents and international department officials from eight countries, including some outside Asia,” he said.

“While I haven’t received any formal endorsements yet, I’m getting a positive response. Since time is short and I don’t want to be held up by incomplete paperwork, I want to secure support from at least six associations.”

Tashima requires nominations from five national associations, a prerequisite for standing in the election.

Candidates have until November 18 to submit nominations for the election, in which Infantino is seeking a fourth term as head of world football’s governing body.

Infantino came under scrutiny in July after an unsuccessful attempt to bring private investors into a new FIFA commercial entity holding rights linked to competitions including the World Cup.

Despite the criticism, Infantino’s candidacy received a significant boost in October when the head of Asian football publicly endorsed him, while support from several FIFA confederations has left him well placed among the organisation’s 211 member associations.

“I’ll keep what’s good and change what’s bad…,” Tashima added. “The biggest problem, however, remains governance…

“Selflessness is my motto… At this stage, I think my chances of winning are about 20 to 30 percent, but as the campaign progresses, I want to raise my confidence to 40 or 50 percent. I truly want to change FIFA.”

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega was the first candidate to publicly declare his intention to challenge fellow Swiss citizen Infantino last month.

news.originalContent:
Protesters seek tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.

Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.

“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.

Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.

Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.

A “ceasefire” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.

The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.

Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.

He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

news.originalContent:
Celebrations feature fireworks, prayers, reunions, rangoli designs, feasting, and the sharing of sweets and gifts.

Diwali, the festival of lights, is being celebrated across India and among its vast diaspora, marking one of the most important days of the year for Hindus.

More than one billion people of different faiths take part in the celebrations in the world’s most populous nation, gathering for prayers, family reunions and the lighting of fireworks.

The name Diwali comes from “Deepavali”, meaning “a row of lights”, and many families place clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance.

The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar and usually falls in late October or early November. This year, Diwali is marked on November 8.

While Diwali is rooted in Hindu tradition, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, with regional origin stories that share a common theme – the victory of good over evil.

Celebrations often include feasting, new clothes, rangoli floor designs, and the exchange of sweets and gifts with friends and neighbours.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Jon Rahm fought off Ryder Cup teammates Rory McIlroy and Tyrrell Hatton to win the Abu Dhabi Championship on Sunday for his first European tour title in four years, marking a successful start to the Spaniard’s career rebuild following the demise of LIV Golf.

Rahm shot 5-under 67 and was 23-under par for the week at Yas Links, two strokes clear of Hatton (68) and four ahead of McIlroy (69) in the first of the two season-ending playoff tournaments in the United Arab Emirates.

This was Rahm’s first event in seven weeks, during which time his wife gave birth to their second daughter — their fourth child — and he set about finalizing a departure from LIV that will see him giving up millions of dollars owed to him.

With LIV this week announcing plans to wind down operations anyway, Rahm is sure to be heading back to the established tours for next season — and has a big win to bring with him for what he acknowledged was a new stage in his life.

“After everything that’s gone on,” Rahm said, “and some poor play and some battles mentally with a lot of noise, to come back out after a bit of rest and being with the family, it’s quite special.”

His last victory on the European tour’s regular circuit was the World Tour Championship in November 2022, which was followed by a green jacket at the Masters a few months later and then the world No. 1 ranking before a controversial move to LIV.

His peerless iron play this week suggests a return to his 2021-23 level, when he collected his two major titles. It was certainly too good for McIlroy and their rivals in an exciting final round at Yas Links.

At one stage early in the back nine, Rahm, McIlroy, Hatton and Francesco Laporta were tied for the lead on 20 under, only for Rahm to pull away with three birdies in a five-hole span from No. 11.

McIlroy’s Sunday charge, which started with a birdie and an eagle on his first two holes of the day, slowed with a bogey at No. 15, while Laporta — chasing his first title — fell out of contention with a triple-bogey at the short par-3 13th. The Italian wound up shooting 72 and finished alone in fourth, six strokes behind Rahm.

Hatton, meanwhile, kept his card clean but couldn’t make enough birdies to reel in Rahm, who walked down the par-5 18th with a two-shot lead and played it safe to make par.

“As far as I’m concerned, except the (tee) shot on No. 17, I played a pretty flawless round,” said Rahm, who banked a winner’s check of $1.5 million. “It was really, really something.”

Two former LIV players finishing 1-2 is perhaps a sign of things to come on the European tour, with many wanting to come back to their roots after the end of the breakaway circuit that once was fueled by Saudi cash.

McIlroy’s disappointment at failing to win will have been slightly tempered by his surge in the season-long Race to Dubai standings.

With his third-place finish, the world No. 2 moved above Patrick Reed and into second place, behind only Eugenio Chacarra with one event left — the World Tour Championship in Dubai starting Thursday.

Chacarra, a 26-year-old Spaniard in his first full season on the tour, finished tied for 22nd this week and Reed tied for 43rd in the 70-man field.

McIlroy is almost 534 points behind Chacarra, with 2,000 on offer for the winner next week and then 1,335 up for grabs for second place and 752 for third place.

McIlroy is looking to join Colin Montgomerie on a record eight Race to Dubai titles. In the Scot’s day, it was called the Order of Merit.

As for this week in Abu Dhabi, getting a two-shot penalty — turning a double-bogey 6 to an 8 — on Thursday hurt McIlroy’s chances. Still, he was encouraged by his performance.

“It was a week where I had my chances,” McIlroy said.

“I would have loved to have won the tournament, but enough positive signs to feel good going into next week.”

Rahm moved up to No. 6 in the Race to Dubai standings so there is an outside chance that he could win the season-long race. One thing is for sure: he would need to win on the Earth course next week to have any hope.

“Actually gives me a little extra incentive next week,” he said. “I really didn’t think I was going to have a chance. Those are better odds than I expected.”

Oakland International Airport is giving bargain hunters a chance to live out their airport-ramp fantasies — if they have a bit of cash.

More than a dozen pint-sized electric tractors, normally used to haul luggage carts and cargo around airport runways, have hit government auction sites for around $750 apiece. The tugs have unexpectedly become social media sensations, with users dreaming up all sorts of ways to put the quirky rides to work.

“They sell for next to nothing,” businessman Shannon Jean tweeted. “What’s the use case for making money, entrepreneur?”

The listings, which include several older models from Oakland’s airport, have sparked a frenzy of jokes from people imagining themselves cruising around their neighborhoods in the unusual vehicles.

“I’d buy one for $700 just to cruise around the neighborhood. Need a lift like 3 blocks away? I gotchu,” one Reddit user wrote.

“Someone should get one for an Austin Powers costume. Drive the kids around in it on Halloween,” another suggested.

“Finally something to tow my mother in law around,” a third joked.

“Imagine the aura of driving one of these around your neighborhood,” Colin Stroud wrote on LinkedIn.

Others fantasized about taking the bargain rides on road trips, although there’s one major catch: These things aren’t exactly built for speed.

Baggage tugs typically travel at just 4 to 15 mph, depending on the model and whether they’re electric or gas-powered. That could make a cross-country adventure a painfully slow proposition.

The Post reached out to Oakland International Airport for comment, but the sales appear to be part of a routine fleet retirement.

Oakland Airport is auctioning off these electric baggage tugs.They sell for next to nothing.What's the use case for making money, Entrepreneur? pic.twitter.com/v00NJnSB0T

Government agencies and municipal airports regularly auction off aging ground-support equipment as it reaches the end of its service life. The Oakland listings appear to include 2008 models.

And the airport isn’t alone in unloading its heavy machinery.

Auction sites also feature a diesel-powered cargo loader in Indiana going for $4,500, while Boise Airport appears to be selling several baggage tractors for just $500 apiece.

One social media user even shared a potential alternative use for the machines, explaining that his family once converted a baggage tug into a snowplow for their long driveway.

“We had one we put a snow plow on to do our long driveway. Had a pretty common Ford 4cyl engine so was easy to maintain,” the user said. “That and my dad worked as an airport equipment mechanic for many years.”

He’s raking in the big bucks.

Lamar Odom earned $50,000 eight days after launching his OnlyFans account, sources told TMZ.

The outlet reported that the former Los Angeles Lakers star is on track to make $200,000 on the subscription-based platform.

“The response to my OnlyFans has been incredible,” Odom told Page Six in a statement.

“I’m connecting with fans in a whole new way, building something big, and now I’m looking to bring other athletes along for the ride,” he added.

“There’s a real opportunity here, and I’m just getting started.”

Last month, the two-time NBA champion, 47, announced he was launching an OnlyFans account, becoming the first NBA star to join.

“On The LO!!” his bio reads. “You’ve seen me on the court. You’ve seen me on TV. Now get to know the REAL me.”

Start your day with Page Six Daily.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Want celebrity news as it breaks?

Odom’s bio added that his account would be “a little more personal,” “a little more playful” and would show a side of the former athlete that fans “haven’t seen before.”

Odom played coy about what he was going to share with his subscribers, who pay $14.99 per month.

“I’ve lived a pretty wild life, and trust me, there are still a few surprises left,” he told TMZ. “I’ve always been an open book, but there are some chapters people haven’t seen yet.”

The former Miami Heat player reportedly made $110 million on salary alone during his NBA career, per Forbes.

However, Odom began having financial issues when he suffered a near-fatal overdose in 2015. To assist with the mounting medical bills, the dad of two pawned his NBA championship rings that he got with the Lakers in 2009 and 2010.

Odom revealed in 2022 that the fan who bought the rings gave them back to him for free.

In March, Odom exclusively told Page Six that he was almost two months sober from alcohol and marijuana.

news.originalTitle: Shoppers flee as gunman unloads rampage of bullets at Krakow’s Main Market Square in Poland
news.title: Shoppers flee as gunman unloads rampage of bullets at Krakow’s Main Market Square in Poland
news.originalSummary: Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said. The gunman, a Polish citizen, aimed at random people as he drove into the Main Square, a major tourist destination in the center of the city, Krakow police said. Police officers are among the wounded.

The Issue: The 2026 election results and what’s now ahead for both Democrats and Republicans.

Many of the Democrats elected in the midterms don’t have a solid proposal to solve the issues they campaigned on (“Stox in AI meltdown,” Nov. 6).

Gas prices won’t drop, borders won’t open and ICE won’t be dismantled like they promised — especially with President Trump holding veto power.

Democrats are about to walk through a revolving door.

Hating the president for today’s prices overlooks who created the mess in the first place.

Trump doesn’t understand what it means to be president.

We witnessed an election turn on one buzzword: “affordability.” But did any Democrat put forth a valid plan on how they would make gas and groceries less expensive?

We’re about to find out what happens when people vote on the “affordability” buzz word.

Republicans: You know what you did wrong; now pull up your bloomers and get to work.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Heart-pounding footage captured the moment a hero Polish cop took down a mass shooter who killed six people in Krakow’s historic market square Saturday in what officials are calling a terror attack, according to reports.

Now, he is fighting for his life — and the country’s leaders are calling for people to donate blood to help him.

Harrowing video shows two officers confront the 24-year-old gunman — who also allegedly murdered his parents and sister at their home — and exchange gunfire in the street at close distance.

One officer, Jakub Kulik, stands over the masked man in full tactical gear and fires multiple shots at him while he’s on the ground, the video shows.

He keeps his gun drawn before he collapses from his own injuries and rolls on his back.

Kulik is a veteran of of Poland’s elite 6th Airborne Brigade, according to Polish media.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek posted on social media: “An urgent appeal for blood for our hero from Kraków.

“Senior Constable Jakub Kulik, who today confronted an armed attacker without hestition, is now fighting for his life in hospital.

“One of his lungs is not functioning, and he needs every drop of blood he can get.”

The two officers rushed to the scene and engaged the gunman within three minutes of him opening fire, authorities said.

The two cops Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Moranski, remain in serious condition Sunday, with one of them still in a coma, officials said.

The suspect was eventually taken into custody and was also hospitalized in critical condition.

The haunting scenes unfolded near the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, where police stopped the gunman after he shot dead four men and two women, one of which was a UK citizen. At least 15 others were injured, officials said, although it’s not clear how many were shot.

Żurek said on X Sunday that the shooter, who has not been identified, “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence.”

“Senior constable Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Moranski are true heroes,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, appearing to refer to both policemen seen in the footage.

Regional governor Krzysztof Klęczar told reporters at a news conference Sunday that without “the efficient and selfless intervention” of the officers, “the number of victims could have been significantly higher.”

“The condition of the two police officers remains serious,” he said, adding that “one of them has already been brought out of a coma while the other remains in a coma and is under medical care.”

The gunman held “very radical and  “ultra-nationalistic” views, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński told reporters.

“Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Tusk revealed that authorities discovered the bodies of three of the suspect’s parents and sister inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 93 miles northeast of Krakow, Poland’s second-largest city.

Gunshots rang out in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town and is a major tourist hub, around 3 p.m. sending people in the area running for their lives.

He went on a “wild ride” driving to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon,  Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.

The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, according to Cisło. Police found other weapons and ammunition in his car.

He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.

Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday.

news.originalContent:
Philippine’ tennis star Eala was left stunned after a 6-3, 6-0 loss to the 102-ranked American in Hong Kong.

Tennis trailblazer Alex Eala from the Philippines burst into tears as she reflected on a “life-changing” season after falling agonisingly short of a second WTA Tour title in Hong Kong.

The second seed was stunned 6-3, 6-0 by Claire Liu in the final of the Hong Kong Open as the American, ranked 102nd, won her first tour title on Sunday.

Eala is at a career-high 17 in the world after a breakout year in which the 21-year-old clinched her maiden title, in Washington, DC, in August.

That victory made her the first player from the Philippines to win a tournament on the WTA Tour.

Eala, set to rise to world number 15 next week, started the year ranked 50th.

“This season has changed my life; it’s changed my life for the better,” Eala, who finished the final with heavy strapping on her right leg, told the crowd afterwards.

Becoming emotional as she addressed her team in the stands, she said: “I’m incredibly proud of the work we’ve put in this year.

“We’re the only ones that truly know what it took to arrive to this point in our journey.

“This is only the beginning.”

news.originalContent:
As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’.

As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea.

With it, the US military ⁠⁠⁠⁠is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.

The same day, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced ambitious plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. That announcement came amid reports of ongoing construction near Iranian missile bases, based on satellite imagery and previous claims by Tehran that US strikes failed to destroy its underground facilities.

Here’s what we know about the US task force:

Task Force Iron Gate will aim to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

It expands on the US blockade of Iranian ports to cover Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea and will reportedly be run by 20 civilian and military personnel.

Iran shares borders with seven countries – Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan Turkiye and Turkmenistan.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said. Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

If US President Donald Trump ramps up the war, there will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”, said Mulroy.

“Unlike Operation Epic Fury, which primarily (focused) on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy said. “It’s primarily a coordination body that’s looking for how the US can increase its economic strangulation strategy by going after the ground routes as they’ve already covered a majority of the maritime routes.”

The IRGC dismissed the US military plan as “just a play on words”.

“The Americans cannot achieve their goal through this, which is to apply severe economic pressure to collapse and disintegrate the Iranian economy,” said IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi, as reported by the Fars news agency.

Washington previously “claimed that Iran will suffer an economic collapse within two weeks, but we witnessed that this did not happen”, he added.

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that reports of military equipment imported via Russia are a “real concern” for the United States.

The task force therefore could “cause a confrontation with Russia”, he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center in Washington, said of the new unit: “The US really doesn’t quite know what to do about Iran as we’ve seen, and it’s doing things off the cuff” – a strategy that has led to little success.

Khouri pointed to Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years as evidence that the US mission is near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia –  it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

While the US can impose a blockade or sanctions on Iran, it cannot control the behaviour of everyone from the Russians, to the Chinese, to the Emiratis and beyond, said the analyst.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

A lot of the materials that go into Iran’s weapons systems are bought from some other countries, – some even from the US or Europeans – and then they are channelled through companies in Asia, Khouri added.

Former Trump aide and top counterterrorism official Joe Kent, who resigned in March due to the US’s war on Iran, said the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent posted on X. “This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

According to The Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM chief Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

The task force may also just be symbolic because the US has no military presence on the Caspian Sea, said Zweiri.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” he said. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

Zweiri also said that the Caspian Sea’s contribution to Iran’s economy is just 11 percent, so the task force’s actions won’t have much negative impact on Tehran.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify this figure but the Caspian Sea accounts for only a fraction of Iran’s overall maritime trade, according to the Soufan Center based in New York City.

A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has sunk off northwestern Senegal, killing at least 21 people.

news.originalContent:
Former rivals in Libya are pushing for a unity government to end years of conflict.

The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns.

Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.

Egypt was widely considered to be backing the eastern authority, effectively led by strongman and renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, and his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), until recent regional developments led Cairo to rethink its approach.

Libyan political analyst Hazem al-Rayes said the reopening of the embassy in Tripoli – which was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar was fighting – is a sign of this.

“I can consider that what Egypt is doing in its recent moves towards the capital, Tripoli, is an attempt to readjust its behaviour in the Libyan file … [for] five years, no Egyptian foreign minister visited the capital,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elias al-Barouni, a political science professor at Libya’s Nalut University, also believes the move goes beyond the resumption of regular consular services in Tripoli.

“We are facing an indicator of a shift in Cairo’s method of managing its relations with the Libyan parties, and a rearrangement of its priorities in dealing with the Libyan crisis,” al-Barouni told Al Jazeera.

There have been several significant political and regional shifts that have somewhat stabilised the volatile situation in Libya, where thousands have been killed in fighting between militias attached to rival political authorities.

In July 2026, Ankara and the LNA reached unprecedented coordination, spearheading agreements to develop military facilities, advanced surveillance systems, and training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers.

The deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, has also paid visits to regional capitals, including Turkiye and Qatar, which have supported the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli.

In Libya, rivals recently signed the so-called “4+4 agreement” that sets out a roadmap for possible presidential and legislative elections over the next two years.

Badr Hassan al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Egypt came to revisit its policy towards Libya after realising that its reliance on eastern forces, led by Haftar, was not conducive to its overall strategic interests.

“It is clear that Cairo … found that relying on one party or leaning towards one party in Libya, which is Haftar’s party, may not be the right bet perhaps at the present time or even for a while, since the Turkish intervention several years ago,” al-Shafei told Al Jazeera.

“Consequently, perhaps Egypt wants to create a balance or also send a message to Haftar that he should not act unilaterally and that acting should be in coordination with Cairo, so it worked to extend bridges of cooperation with Libya also …”

Egypt has also become more concerned about developments to the south of its border, particularly the expansion of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, which had allegedly received support from Haftar.

“Today, Egypt is no longer the Egypt of five years ago when its policies and relations were limited only to the [eastern] authorities in Benghazi,” al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

It is “convinced today that its ally [LNA], which it supported throughout the past years at the expense of the legitimate government in Tripoli … has distanced itself from it today, and it needs to readjust its political behaviour with Tripoli and with the legitimate government”, he said.

During Abdelatty’s visit to Tripoli, he discussed critical economic files with Libyan officials, including the 2019 maritime border memorandum of understanding signed between Tripoli and Ankara.

According to the Facebook page of the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Abdelatty reaffirmed the importance of addressing Egyptian concerns regarding maritime demarcation between Libya and Turkiye in light of international law. The eastern parliament recently ratified the maritime agreement, which it initially opposed.

“Consequently, perhaps Cairo is trying to prevent the ratification of this agreement from causing damage to its interests in gas and oil exploration in the Eastern Mediterranean, and from that it wanted to extend bridges to Tripoli as well,” al-Shafei said.

“Instead of limiting itself to political and diplomatic objection from outside Tripoli, Cairo has become negotiating directly with the Libyan government that signed the agreement.”

Egypt might also be attracted to opportunities that reconstruction and the revival of Libya’s oil industry might bring.

“Perhaps with the reconstruction process, the incoming Egyptian labour will have priority, or even the currently present one will have its living conditions improved, not to mention the idea of the possibility of Egyptian investments and companies entering the reconstruction process,” al-Shafei said.

After years of backing rival sides, a new regional consensus means there is a greater likelihood of rivals in Libya reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the war, al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

But al-Barouni cautioned that there is still a plethora of issues facing Libya, and only a comprehensive solution can end the divisions within Libya.

“The Libyan problem is not merely a dispute over the name of the head of government, but rather it is a dispute over the nature of power, the distribution of influence, control over institutions and resources, the future of the military institution, and the conditions for reaching elections,” al-Barouni said.

“If Cairo, Ankara, Washington, and other capitals agree on the necessity of ending the division, that is a development that can be built upon, but the success of any settlement remains linked to the ability of the Libyans to formulate an independent national project. Libya needs a settlement that ends the division, not a deal that redistributes the division.”

news.originalContent:
A political impasse between the KRG and PUK threatens to break up the semiautonomous northern region into zones of governance.

Disagreements between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) over the formation of a new government have led to the threat of two rival administrations emerging in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq, analysts say.

The dispute between the two dominant political forces in the semiautonomous Kurdistan Regional Government, which traditionally has operated under a power-sharing agreement, escalated after a parliamentary session was held last week in Erbil without the PUK’s participation.

PUK leader Bafel Talabani responded by withdrawing his party from the government, and a threat is growing that a rival administration could be formed in the party’s Sulaimaniyah base.

Independent Kurdish politician Yasin Aziz said the latest developments have deepened the historical divisions between the KDP and PUK.

“I believe the spectre of two administrations in Kurdistan is now very close, and the outlines of such a scenario are becoming clear. … The events have been painful and rapid. The differences between the two parties were significant and have now led to a breakdown in relations,” Aziz told Al Jazeera.

“There had been hopes that the two sides would reach an agreement, but activating parliament without the PUK deepened the divisions between the KDP and PUK.”

The KDP, which is led by Massoud Barzani, is the biggest party in the region, and its strongholds are in Erbil and Dohuk.

Since the first Gulf War in 1990 and 1991 and the establishment of a US-led “no-fly zone” in northern Iraq, Iraq’s Kurds have largely governed themselves, separate from the national government in Baghdad.

The Iraqi Constitution enacted after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq recognised the northern Kurdish region as a federal entity with its own legislative, executive and judicial powers.

There is a historical precedent for the possible separation of powers in this region between two rival authorities. When a conflict erupted between elements of the KDP and PUK in the 1990s, the two parties formed separate local governments in Erbil and Sulaimaniyah, respectively.

While there have been no recent violent flare-ups between the two parties, political distrust remains deep.

During the sixth parliamentary elections in the region on October 20, 2024, the KDP won 39 seats and the PUK 23. This left a 16-seat gap between the two parties.

But the KDP’s ability to form a new government was still dependent on reaching an agreement with the PUK and other parties, such as the New Generation Movement, which secured 15 seats in the last election.

The PUK has so far refused to collaborate, so after a two-year wait, the KDP reactivated the regional parliament on Wednesday without its rivals.

Although the rivalry between the two parties is longstanding, Aziz argued that the current crisis is more serious and deeply rooted than previous political disputes.

“Given the political stubbornness of both parties, I do not expect an agreement or understanding to be reached soon,” he said. “Both sides must make concessions to each other. The party willing to make greater concessions will demonstrate greater concern for the Kurdistan region.”

Aziz was clear in laying blame for the deepening divide.

“The responsibility for deepening this conflict lies with the leaderships of Kurdistan’s two main parties,” he said. “Their failure to recognise the risks posed by continuing these disputes is one of the reasons we have reached this point.”

Subhi Mandalawi, a member of the KDP, blamed the current impasse on the refusal of the PUK to form a new government with the KDP.

“Following the Kurdistan parliamentary elections, the PUK delayed the formation of the new government. They were counting on the KDP being unable to secure the legal quorum needed to convene a parliamentary session,” Mandalawi told Al Jazeera. “But we held a parliamentary session without the PUK in 2018 as well, and they subsequently joined the government and parliament.”

Mandalawi insisted that the door remains open for the PUK and other political parties but warned that prolonged divisions would lead to deeper problems for the Kurdish region.

“Continuing to obstruct legislative institutions two years after the elections is unacceptable and harms the Kurdistan region domestically, regionally and internationally,” he said.

“Threatening to divide the Kurdistan region is a hasty, ill-considered and unrealistic decision. No party leader can take such a step, and the PUK would be the biggest loser if it went ahead with it.”

Despite the differences, there is little risk of a return to conflict between the two parties. “We are brothers, and there can be no fighting among us,” Mandalawi said.

Mahmood Khoshnaw, a senior PUK official, said the KDP’s decision to convene parliament without his party has worsened political tensions in the region.

“Activating parliament without the PUK represents a departure from the principle of partnership and from political realities, and there will be consequences. If a prime minister is appointed in Erbil, we will take the same step in Sulaimaniyah. Whatever the KDP does, we will do the same in Sulaimaniyah,” Khoshnaw warned.

“The situation in the Kurdistan region is heading towards chaos unless the crisis is addressed rationally and realistically. Activating parliament without reaching an understanding with the PUK has had a negative impact on relations between the two parties.”

Despite this, there are questions about whether Sulaimaniyah could legally separate from the Kurdish regional government.

Ramadan Albadran, an independent political analyst and constitutional affairs expert, said the dispute is not a constitutional issue about the KDP’s convening of parliament but a deep political crisis with the potential to create security repercussions for the region.

The Iraqi constitution also provides no mechanism for dividing the region into zones of influence between the KDP and PUK.

“If the PUK moves to separate Sulaimaniyah from the Kurdistan region, that would not be a legal or constitutional act,” Albadran said.

“If it takes place without a mandate from the elected Kurdistan Regional Government, it would be closer to an act of rebellion since there is no legal provision permitting withdrawal from or the dismantling of a region in this manner.”

news.originalContent:
‘Terrorism’ investigation launched after government officials say suspect likely influenced by far-right ideology.

Poland has begun two days of national mourning after an armed man killed six people in central Krakow, as the national prosecutor’s office opened a “terrorism” investigation.

The 24-year-old Polish suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakow’s historic city centre. A British national was among those killed, according to police, and nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia were among the 15 wounded, authorities told the PAP news agency.

Three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, about 150km (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Police said they were his parents and a sister.

The suspect was also wounded during police action and is in critical condition in hospital.

Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office said on social media on Sunday it had “launched an investigation today into yesterday’s attack in Krakow”, adding it was probing “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

Daniel Prokopowicz, a spokesperson for the office, said it was “highly likely” that the killings in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski and Krakow were carried out by the same person, but that investigations were ongoing.

According to media reports, the suspect, Michal O, had a valid gun licence and no prior criminal record.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski stated the attacker was influenced by far-right and ultranationalist ideologies and views.

Meanwhile, Krakow’s main market square and ⁠the surrounding streets remained closed on Sunday, with police allowing only essential service workers.

Many nearby cafes were closed and flags ⁠at the city hall were at half-mast. Mourners placed candles in several locations in the area.

The traditional hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s church on the square was suspended for 12 hours to commemorate the dead, the first time this has happened since 1939, the Polish Press Agency reported.

news.originalContent:
اسحاق هرتسوگ، رئیس‌جمهور اسرائیل، پس از رایزنی با رهبران احزاب سیاسی، گادی آیزنکوت را برای تشکیل دولت جدید انتخاب کرده است. قرار است حکم رسمی ماموریت او روز یکشنبه اعطا شود. این تصمیم در حالی گرفته شده که هیچ‌یک از ائتلاف‌های اصلی در انتخابات اخیر نتوانسته‌اند اکثریت لازم را در پارلمان به دست آورند.

هرتسوگ گفت که در رایزنی‌های انجام‌شده، گادی آیزنکوت، رهبر بلوک مخالف دولت بنیامین نتانیاهو، بیشترین حمایت نمایندگان احزاب را برای تشکیل دولت به دست آورده است.

دفتر ریاست‌جمهوری اسرائیل در بیانیه‌ای اعلام کرد: «رئیس‌جمهور، گادی آیزنکوت، رهبر حزب یاشار، را از تصمیم خود برای مامور کردن او به تشکیل دولت مطلع کرده است.»

در این بیانیه آمده است که حکم رسمی ماموریت تشکیل دولت روز یکشنبه، طی مراسمی در اقامتگاه ریاست‌جمهوری در بیت‌المقدس، به آیزنکوت اعطا خواهد شد.

در انتخابات ۲۷ اکتبر اسرائیل، حزب لیکود به رهبری بنیامین نتانیاهو با کسب ۲۷ کرسی به بزرگ‌ترین حزب پارلمان تبدیل شد، اما ائتلاف احزاب ملی‌گرا و مذهبی حامی او در مجموع تنها ۵۳ کرسی از ۱۲۰ کرسی کنست را به دست آورد.

چهار حزب تشکیل‌دهنده بلوک مخالف به رهبری آیزنکوت نیز ۴۸ کرسی کسب کردند. حزب یاشار به رهبری او با ۲۱ کرسی دومین حزب بزرگ پارلمان شد.

در این میان، دو حزب نماینده شهروندان عرب اسرائیل در مجموع ۱۹ کرسی به دست آوردند؛ رقمی بی‌سابقه که می‌تواند به آنها نقشی تعیین‌کننده در تشکیل دولت جدید بدهد.

اگرچه آیزنکوت تاکنون از ائتلاف با احزاب عرب خودداری کرده است، رهبران این احزاب در رایزنی‌های خود با رئیس‌جمهور از مأمور شدن او برای تشکیل دولت حمایت کردند. همین حمایت باعث شد که آیزنکوت بیشترین توصیه‌ها را از سوی نمایندگان پارلمان دریافت کند.

آیزنکوت پس از اعلام تصمیم رئیس‌جمهور در شبکه ایکس نوشت: «اکنون زمان تشکیل دولت اضطراری ملی است. تمام تلاشم را خواهم کرد تا شایسته این مسئولیت باشیم.»

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

آیزنکوت پس از دریافت حکم رسمی، ۲۸ روز فرصت خواهد داشت تا برای تشکیل دولت به توافق برسد. این مهلت ممکن است ۱۴ روز دیگر تمدید شود.

یکی از گزینه‌های پیش روی او تشکیل دولتی اقلیت با حمایت احزاب عرب در رای‌گیری‌های کلیدی پارلمان است. جلب حمایت احزاب مذهبی یهودیان ارتدوکس افراطی یا تشکیل دولت وحدت ملی با نتانیاهو نیز از دیگر گزینه‌های احتمالی به شمار می‌روند.

با این حال، آیزنکوت پیش‌تر اعلام کرده است که حاضر نیست در دولتی به همراه نتانیاهو حضور داشته باشد. تحلیلگران نیز دستیابی به توافق بر سر هر یک از این گزینه‌ها را دشوار ارزیابی می‌کنند.

اگر آیزنکوت موفق به تشکیل دولت نشود، فرصت به نامزد دیگری داده خواهد شد. در صورت ادامه بن‌بست سیاسی و ناکامی تلاش‌های بعدی، احتمال برگزاری انتخابات مجدد وجود دارد.

ساعتی پیش از اعلام تصمیم هرتسوگ، بنیامین نتانیاهو، نخست‌وزیر اسرائیل، هشدار داد که تشکیل ائتلافی احتمالی میان احزاب مخالف و احزاب عرب که او آنها را «اسلام‌گرا» نامید، به فروپاشی کشور منجر خواهد شد.

نتانیاهو در یک سخنرانی ویدیویی از پیش ضبط‌شده گفت: «چنین دولتی که به اسلام‌گرایان وابسته باشد، کشور اسرائیل را از درون متلاشی خواهد کرد، همان‌طور که این اتفاق در کشورهای اروپایی در حال وقوع است، و حتی بسیار بدتر از آن.»

آیزنکوت ۶۶ ساله، فرمانده پیشین ارتش اسرائیل است که در سال ۲۰۲۲ وارد عرصه سیاست شد. او پس از حمله حماس به اسرائیل در هفتم اکتبر ۲۰۲۳ برای مدتی در کابینه جنگی نتانیاهو حضور داشت، اما بعد به صف مخالفان دولت بازگشت.

او در سال‌های اخیر با انتقاد از نحوه مدیریت جنگ غزه از سوی نتانیاهو، خشونت شهرک‌نشینان اسرائیلی علیه فلسطینیان را نیز محکوم کرده است.

آیزنکوت که پسر و دو برادرزاده‌اش را در جنگ غزه از دست داده، در مبارزات انتخاباتی بر سوابق نظامی و امنیتی خود تاکید کرده است.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)

Houston police will no longer alert federal immigration agents during routine traffic stops, three days after Democrats swept every statewide office in Texas.

Democratic Mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order Friday narrowing when officers may contact Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Two conditions must now apply together. The person has to be arrested on a jailable charge and has to carry an ICE administrative warrant, according to the Texas Tribune. Officers will cite and release people in minor nonviolent cases.

Whitmire tied the switch to Tuesday’s results. “If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse,” he said in an interview with The New York Times. “We just are not going to deal with the nonviolent contacts.” (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Trump ‘Will Never Allow For Mass Amnesty’ After Floating Working With Dems On Immigration)

Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law, bars police departments from limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities, the Tribune reported. Whitmire voted against that bill as a state lawmaker. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office in January.

Rather, it was that Hutton was skating on the left side of Matt Kessel against the Devils and not Scott Mayfield, who was a healthy scratch.

While Mayfield has been fighting what looks more and more like an uphill battle for his spot on the depth chart since training camp, it would be hard to argue he hasn’t outplayed Kessel lately and harder still to argue that his importance to the penalty kill doesn’t justify keeping him in the lineup until Ryan Pulock returns from an upper-body injury.

In the first three games since Pulock’s injury, Mayfield has been the Islanders ice-time leader at 4-on-5, as the penalty kill had gone 10-for-11.

That felt extra prescient as the Islanders skated on the penalty kill four times in a 5-4 overtime defeat, using just three defensemen at 4-on-5 while leaning heavily on Logan Stanley and Adam Pelech — both of whom took penalties themselves.

“He’s a part of [the penalty kill],” coach Pete DeBoer said of Mayfield before the game. “When you make those decisions, guys come out and we’re well aware of some of the strengths of the guys coming out. Also some of the strengths of guys going in. I think if we take five or six penalties tonight we’re in trouble anyway. We gotta stay out of the box.”

Afterward, he praised the job the PK did and said, “All penalty killers get fatigued,” when there are that many opportunities.

Though Mayfield and general manager Mathieu Darche have both dismissed trade rumors surrounding him, this does come against the backdrop of those rumors as well — as well as a looming roster crunch once the Islanders, currently one player short of the roster limit, activate all three of Mathew Barzal, Matias Maccelli and Calum Ritchie.

Barzal and Maccelli were both full participants at Saturday’s optional morning skate and could be back soon, but the Islanders could stave off waiving someone once that happens by moving Ryan Pulock to injured reserve.

Mayfield can’t be traded without his consent, but he could be waived, and the Islanders could wield that weapon to get him to agree to a trade, a move the Rangers controversially employed to get Jacob Trouba to waive his no-trade clause a couple of years ago.

DeBoer did not have an answer following the game on whether Barzal or Maccelli would travel with the team to San Jose on Sunday, saying he needed to meet with the medical staff.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Three teenagers and an adult have been charged with murder in Georgia after a mother found her 15-year-old son shot to death inside an abandoned residence following Halloween night.

The Albany Police Department said investigators arrested 22-year-old Detravion Parke, as well as two 15-year-olds and a 16-year-old in connection with the death of Austin Payne, 15.

All four suspects were charged with murder and transported to the Dougherty County Jail, according to police.

Officers responded to the 800 block of Cameo Lane in Albany on Nov. 1, where they discovered Payne dead inside an abandoned home, police said.

His mother found him by tracking his location via cellphone after he failed to return home on Halloween, according to WALB.

Albany Police Chief Michael Persley said during a Nov. 2 news conference that Payne had contacted his mother after being shot.

“He did make a call to his mother that he had been shot,” Persley said.

According to WALB, investigators reviewed surveillance footage, cellphone records and witness statements to reconstruct the events leading up to Payne’s death.

Witnesses told investigators that armed individuals approached a group walking with Payne, demanded their belongings and opened fire, the outlet reported.

Payne may have been targeted during an attempted robbery involving a handgun he had recently displayed on social media, according to WALB.

Payne’s family has launched a GoFundMe fundraiser to help cover funeral expenses following his death.

A relative said Payne would have turned 16 on Nov. 12.

“Our family is trying to process this heartbreaking loss,” the relative wrote.

The fundraiser also noted that Payne is survived by his mother and 17-year-old sister.

The Albany Police Department is asking anyone with additional information about the shooting to contact investigators at 229-431-2100.

news.originalContent:

ATLANTA — Understand that “back” is the worst four-letter word for Nets fans.

They read about back woes, minutes limits and injury management, but Ben Simmons is what they see. And what they fear.

But with Mikel Brown Jr., they don’t have to be afraid.

Despite the kid gloves the Nets have treated their rookie with, Brown’s ankle is fine. And more importantly, so is his back.

While Brown was limited to 21 games for Louisville last season, sources told The Post that his back was structurally fine. That injury had just been a soft tissue one and is long since in the past. His current minutes limit is about the future and building strength for that — for who the Nets see as an eventual All-Star.

“It’s all about getting stronger,” Brown told The Post before scoring 18 points in the Nets’ 124-121 loss to the Hawks on Saturday night. “This is my first year playing against this type of high level of athletes. You’ve got to be at an elite performance level body-wise. But that’s just the everyday process when it comes to that stuff.

“I’m constantly in the weight room every day just strengthening the parts of my body I need to strengthen. But yeah, that’s us going along with the plan. I’m all aboard with it. As long as we’re winning games, that’s all I care about.”

With Brown being the reward for a long tanking season, fans are not only invested in his progress but still scarred from the Simmons experience — trading James Harden for what turned out to be just 90 ineffective games in three seasons.

“Nah, man, that was never the case,” said Brown, who will not play Sunday in Dallas because he’s not cleared for back-to-backs. “I’ve just been leaning on my performance staff. My body feels great. Just take it slow. It’s an 82-game season. We want to be in a position to make the playoffs, so every game matters, but they’re just like, ‘the long run, the long run.’ So taking it a game at a time, a day at a time, and attacking it. Everything’s fine. I don’t look at (social) media like that, but yes, everything’s fine. My body’s great, just continuing to build.”

Brown has yet to play both legs of a back to back, with the Nets to play Sunday in Dallas.

He entered Saturday averaging 12 points and four assists. And the game is visibly slowing down for the rookie, mustering 14.5 points in his last four tilts.

“I’m very happy with Mikel. Him in pick-and-roll, how fast he is, how shifty, he can shoot the 3, get to the rim. Very happy with his performance,” coach Jordi Fernández said.

“It’s always about playing hard, but it’s also about playing smarter as well. So, just really having the game slow down,” Brown told The Post. “I watched a lot of film with my coaches, a whole lot of film for myself, just slowing down and letting the game come to me and just letting the game flow.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter!

“And just staying aggressive, living with the consequences if I turn the ball over, miss an assignment on defense, just knowing I have to get it back the next play. Just always having that next-play mentality. That’s the mindset that’s been in my head these past couple games.”

Brown has particularly excelled in the pick-and-roll, capped by an 18 point, four-assist outing in their win over Charlotte. He shot 6 of 11, 3 of 5 from deep and had a highlight no-look pass to Moritz Wagner off a baseline drive.

“Yeah, really the willingness to just be myself and create plays within that pick-and-roll situation, whether that’s hitting the pocket, reading the tag man. Just allowing the game to come to me. It’s nothing I haven’t worked on for freaking years before this. So I adapt and put it on show,” Brown said.

“Great player. Big-time offensive spark,” said Terance Mann. “He’s gonna be good when he gets older, stronger, understands the game, understands the pick-and-roll situations. I could see him being an All-Star easily. He has a great basketball mind. So, it’s fun to play with him.”

The Nets are strengthening Brown’s body, especially his core, searching for that All-Star outcome.

news.originalContent:
Heavy rain floods tents housing displaced Palestinians in Gaza as Israeli restrictions on aid hamper response.

Heavy rain has flooded tens of thousands of displaced people’s tents in war-devastated Gaza, Palestinian authorities said, leaving many without shelter.

Since early Saturday, displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and other northern areas of the territory, as well as parts of central Gaza, after they were inundated by rainwater.

Gaza authorities said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains.

The statement also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some of them critical, in various areas of the war-devastated territory.

Palestinian Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal told the news agency AFP on Saturday his teams had received more than 1,500 calls during the night from residents requesting urgent assistance after their tents were flooded, explaining that the agency “is operating without any equipment or capabilities”.

“We have issued an urgent distress call to the international community and humanitarian organisations to intervene immediately to save hundreds of thousands of displaced people from the flooding of their tents.”

“We cannot face the consequences of this storm on our own,” Bassal added.

news.originalContent:
JD Vance’s response to the midterm defeat suggests a once-untouchable Republican consensus may be starting to crack.

Washington-based journalist.

The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections may have opened a debate that, until recently, would have been almost unthinkable within the party: whether the United States should fundamentally reconsider its relationship with Israel.

For decades, unwavering support for Israel was a defining feature of Republican identity, sustained by evangelical Christians, the conservative foreign policy establishment, influential lobbying organisations, and a deeply entrenched congressional consensus. Now, following the electorate’s repudiation of Donald Trump and his administration, that consensus is showing unmistakable signs of strain.

The clearest indication came from Vice President JD Vance, who acknowledged in an unusually candid post-election assessment that dissatisfaction with America’s relationship with Israel was among the reasons Republican voters abandoned their party. Identifying four concerns driving former Trump supporters towards Democrats, Vance cited the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, the principle of putting America first, and, significantly, changing the American relationship with Israel.

His admission was remarkable not simply because of what he said, but because of who said it. As the administration’s second-highest official and a potential Republican presidential contender in 2028, Vance effectively acknowledged that unconditional support for the Israeli government is no longer politically cost-free, even within the Republican coalition.

More importantly, he brought into the open a question Republican politicians have traditionally been reluctant to entertain: whether America’s commitment to Israel continues to serve America’s own interests.

Does this represent a genuine reassessment, however, or merely an attempt to explain an electoral disaster and reposition the party for 2028?

There are compelling reasons to believe that something more consequential is under way. The Republican alliance with Israel has rested on several overlapping foundations: evangelical Christian support, strategic and intelligence cooperation, military interests, and conservative political organisations that have made backing Israel an almost unquestionable test of political loyalty.

But those foundations are increasingly being challenged by a younger generation of conservatives, particularly within the emerging America First movement, who question why American resources and military commitments should be directed towards foreign conflicts while economic pressures mount at home.

Their scepticism does not necessarily reflect sympathy for Palestinians or opposition to Israel’s existence. Rather, it challenges the assumption that American and Israeli interests are automatically identical. Increasingly, these voters want to know why Washington should continue providing extensive military assistance, diplomatic protection, and political support regardless of the policies pursued by the Israeli government.

The wars in Gaza and Iran have brought that question into sharper focus. Israel’s devastating military campaign in Gaza, the resulting humanitarian catastrophe, and Washington’s continued military and diplomatic backing have imposed mounting moral, diplomatic, and strategic costs on the United States. The subsequent confrontation with Iran further exposed the dangers of allowing Israeli security priorities and regional calculations to influence American decisions about war and peace.

Vance’s intervention, therefore, did not emerge from a political vacuum. It reflects tensions that have been developing within the Republican electorate for years. Earlier polling had already identified declining enthusiasm for Israel among younger Republicans, even as traditional constituencies remained considerably more supportive. The Chicago Council’s 2026 survey also found declining Republican favourability towards Israel compared with 2022, although Republicans continued to favour maintaining or increasing military assistance. The picture is consequently not of a party abandoning Israel, but of one increasingly divided over the terms and consequences of the relationship.

That division could become central to the Republican Party’s struggle over its post-Trump future. By identifying dissatisfaction with Israel policy as a factor in the electoral losses, Vance has effectively legitimised a debate that conservative politicians have long avoided. He has also signalled that the issue could become an important point of differentiation among potential presidential contenders preparing for 2028.

For Trump, the contradiction is particularly damaging. He built his political movement around putting America first and ending costly foreign entanglements, yet his presidency has become closely associated with extraordinary support for Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, including military cooperation, diplomatic backing, and confrontation with regional adversaries.

The Iran war has made that contradiction harder to defend. Voters who supported Trump expecting him to prioritise domestic concerns may reasonably question why the United States became entangled in another Middle Eastern conflict, particularly when the consequences include economic uncertainty, higher energy costs, and resources diverted from domestic priorities.

While Trump has acknowledged that the Iran conflict contributed to Republican losses, he has continued defending the decision to launch it. The real test, therefore, will not be what Republican politicians say in the aftermath of their defeat, but what they are prepared to do. Will they support conditions on military assistance? And will they recognise that a sustainable regional settlement must address Palestinian freedom, security, and political rights rather than treating them as secondary considerations?

These are the questions that distinguish a genuine reassessment from electoral opportunism.

For Palestinians, the stakes are considerable. But expectations should remain measured. A change in Republican rhetoric does not necessarily translate into a change in America’s strategic priorities, much less an immediate departure from decades of established policy.

Ultimately, the significance of the midterm defeat may lie less in an immediate transformation of American policy than in the erosion of an assumption that has governed Washington for generations: that support for Israel is politically untouchable. The Republican Party now faces a choice: ignore the warning or recognise that its political future may depend, in part, on responding to it.

news.originalContent:
With a decisive rejection of Trumpism, US voters have given Democrats one more chance — they better not blow it.

Political organiser, campaigner, and strategist.

In the days since the midterm elections in the United States, many commentators have argued that the “blue tsunami” signalled a popular rejection of US President Donald Trump, but not a new love for Democrats. They are right to warn that if the Democratic Party fails to deliver, it will likely face the same kind of anti-incumbent anger in the next election cycle.

I have personally spilled loads of ink arguing that the Democratic old guard’s embrace of neoliberalism is a huge part of what created the crisis conditions that enabled Trump’s rise to power in the first place, and has severely hampered their ability to stop him over the past decade.

But this election cycle was different in remarkable ways. To put it in plain terms, the Democrats started “sucking less” — not all of them, but a lot of them. And this recent demonstration of “sucking less” is what is presently providing me with at least an ounce of hope that the party might actually manage not to blow this historic opportunity.

How did the Democrats “suck less”? First off, there was a proliferation of progressive economic populist candidates who explicitly took on powerful corporations and positioned themselves clearly as fighters for working-class people. The economic populist insurgency within the Democratic Party gained significant ground in this cycle.

Some might wonder, what took so long? For one, it’s easy to forget that the electoral insurgency within the GOP had an eight-year head start on the insurgency within the Democratic Party — and that head start has been enormously consequential.

In the wake of the 2008 financial meltdown, it was, ironically, conservative anti-establishment energy that first captured populist momentum through the Tea Party. With the help of organisations such as FreedomWorks, that energy was quickly channelled into Republican Party primary contests. By 2014, Tea Party activists had unseated GOP House Speaker Eric Cantor and set the stage for Trump.

Nearly three years after the Tea Party kicked off, Occupy Wall Street was the left’s opening salvo in the populist era. By framing a popular class conflict (the 99% vs the 1%) and naming popular villains (Wall Street and big banks), Occupy dramatically changed the national “common sense” about the evils of runaway inequality.

But the grassroots movement was allergic to the electoral realm. Senator Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run brought Occupy’s core message onto electoral terrain, but it wasn’t until the 2018 midterms — with the election of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and “the Squad” — that the left’s capacity for electoral insurgency caught up with where the right already was in 2009.

Since then, independent progressive organisations such as Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, and countless local and statewide organisations (for example, PA Stands Up and PA United in my home state of Pennsylvania) have been developing their capacity for recruiting and supporting working-class champions to run for office.

This has been a profound development. Over the course of a decade now, in fits and starts, this groundswell of independent grassroots organising has broken the Democratic Party establishment’s virtual monopoly on candidate recruitment. The 2026 midterms demonstrated a significant increase in capacity to run working-class champions for Congress.

And without diminishing the importance of this long-term organisational investment, it is clear that 2026 also saw an organic proliferation of candidates who ran as champions of the working class. This organic proliferation didn’t happen by chance: It was the result of a profound shift in common-sense notions of what constitutes a winning message.

Over the past decade, a growing chorus of voices in Congress and on the campaign trail has taken up the message Bernie originally popularised, arguing for the same reforms and overhauls, from passing Medicare for All and making housing and childcare affordable, to reining in artificial intelligence (AI) and taxing the rich.

But it took a confluence of events to finally start to break into the mainstream of the Democratic Party in the 2026 cycle.

One key event, unfortunately, was Trump winning a second term. An important casualty of Trump’s second victory was the median Democratic voter’s faith in party leadership. The arc of results and consequences from 2016 to 2024 suddenly cleared the fog, exposing a damning narrative about the party leadership’s negligent qualifications when it came to winning elections.

All that stuff they told us about Bernie being “too far left”, all their wisdom about “electability” was nonsense. The acceleration of the party’s already severe bleed of working-class voters in 2024 and its alarming spread to Black and Latino voters exposed the utter bankruptcy of Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s lauded affluent suburban swing voter strategy.

The next key event was more uplifting, thankfully. In 2025, in a moment when progressive hopes were at their lowest ebb, suddenly Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani showed up out of nowhere with one of the most captivating and inspiring mayoral campaigns in US history, winning the Democratic nomination for mayor of New York City, and then the election.

Mamdani’s incredible message discipline centred around one word: affordability. With a discredited party leadership, mostly missing in action, Mamdani effectively filled a leadership and vision vacuum. Meanwhile, Bernie and AOC were crisscrossing the country, filling stadiums and energising the base with their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.

On the eve of the 2026 midterm season, economic populism had become the only thing on offer, the only thing that seemed to credibly have a chance. Suddenly, a whole lot of Democratic candidates and officeholders were talking about affordability and the working class.

One of the few things party leadership did right in 2026 was not derailing this growing populist message and momentum. So while Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries remain unpopular, a movement among the rank-and-file and a new crop of economic populist candidates managed to land a coherent and compelling narrative.

An orthodox Marxist might argue that the explanation for the Democratic Party’s failure over the past decade to connect to working-class voters is straightforward: It doesn’t want to bite the hand that feeds it, in other words, billionaires and powerful corporations that provide millions in campaign contributions.

While big money undoubtedly provides significant incentives, I take a perspective more like sociologist Max Weber’s, where the political class has an important degree of “relative autonomy”. Most political operatives genuinely want to win elections, but their ideas about how to do so are constrained and distorted by the elite cultural milieu in which they are embedded.

It’s taken a full 10 years since Trump’s first victory for economic populism to finally break into the elite bubble of the liberal consultant class, or at least to bypass it and finally approach a critical mass of candidates and officeholders in the Democratic Party who grasp how the world has changed, what hardship and precarity most Americans are experiencing, and how to win working-class voters back.

In his 2016 run for president, Bernie was not “ahead of his time”. He was reading the times perfectly. What he was ahead of was an out-of-touch Democratic Party establishment, whose misreading of the times enabled a dangerous authoritarian pseudo-populist to ascend to power and set America’s downward spiralling course for a decade now.

Tuesday’s historic “blue tsunami” was not only the result of Trump’s failures. The 2026 midterm election cycle also saw the start of the remaking of the Democratic Party to be a party that — as Bernie steadfastly exhorts us — fights for the working class.

Yes, sure, Bernie probably would have won the general election back in 2016 and 2020. But more to the point today: Bernie is winning. That is to say, by finally moving towards an economic populist agenda and a commitment to America’s working class, the Democratic Party might just be starting to find its popular voice.

Tuesday’s results do not mean US voters have sworn loyalty to the Democratic Party. But they have given it another chance. A chance to deliver and improve people’s lives. It would be wise and electorally prudent to deliver… bigly.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

CLEVELAND — The visitors locker room sounded like a Sweet 16.

The setlist opened with “Shake It Off,” followed by “You Belong With Me,” “Style” and “Bad Blood.”

The Knicks — led by DJ Jalen Brunson — were partying like it was “1989.”

Tyler Kolek — who this week questioned Taylor Swift’s Knicks fandom during an NBA 2K League livestream — may never, ever, ever hear the end of it from Swifties, but the second-year guard was hoping to make amends with one of the world’s biggest stars following the Knicks’ 109-97 win over the Cavaliers.

Kolek had labeled Swift the fakest celebrity Knicks fan on the bandwagon during their title run, calling the musician “performative” after she attended Game 4 of the NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden.

“It’s just a question that was asked for me, that maybe I answered in the wrong way. Take that on the chin,” Kolek said Saturday night. “I love her music. We were just playing it five minutes ago, and I’m singing every word to every song. Nothing against her at all.

“People have been going back and sending me all this stuff about her coming to the games, and she was actually wearing a [No.] 13 jersey [of] Joakim Noah back in the day with Carmelo [Anthony]. That’s on me. I wasn’t up to date on my Taylor Swift Knicks fandom. So that’s on me.”

The previous day, the Knicks put out a statement in support of Swift, whose wedding to Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce was held at the Garden this summer.

“Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization,” a Knicks spokesperson said.

The Knicks returned to Cleveland for the first time since the Eastern Conference finals, when Swift attended Game 3 at Rocket Arena with Kelce — an Ohio native — and was seen cheering for the Cavaliers.

When Kolek called out Swift in the video with teammate Deuce McBride, he acknowledged he was “going to get some hate from the Swifties.”

Since then, his teammates have taken their shots too.

“For sure, they’re playing Taylor Swift in the locker room,” Kolek said. “We were at practice [Friday and] we were playing Taylor. I love her music. I probably know more songs than anybody else in the locker room. Just misspoken.”
